meta.title: Muse Ic music-theory knowledge base
notes: Roots are semitones above the key tonic when relativeTo='key', or above the current chord root when relativeTo='currentChord'.
Quality codes are defined in chordQualities (intervals in semitones above the root).
neoRiemannian = shortest P/L/R path (applied left to right) between the two triads' major/minor cores; null for chords without a clear major/minor triad (sus, dim, aug, power).
moods use ids from moodVocabulary. consensus: high = textbook/widely agreed; medium = common in the literature/genre convention; low = subjective or idiosyncratic.
examples are included only when verified against a cited source (sourceUrl). Empty = not verified, not 'none exist'.
caveats: Mood vocabulary: the 29 core moods were selected by cross-source consensus (Hevner, GEMS/GEMIAC, Last.fm studies, AllMusic/MIREX, Cowen 2020, Spotify/Apple). Most taxonomies are English-language and Western-listener based; Cowen et al. tested US and Chinese listeners only. Valence/arousal/brightness/tension coordinates are compiler placements, not measured values.

Western tonal bias: nearly all categories (Roman numerals, functional harmony, major=happy/minor=sad) come from Western European common-practice, jazz and Anglo-American pop. Other traditions (Indian raga, Arabic maqam, Indonesian gamelan, etc.) organize pitch and emotion differently; a raga's rasa or a maqam's character is not captured here.

Enculturation: mood associations (even major/minor) are largely learned. Cross-cultural studies find some shared cues (e.g., tempo, loudness) but weaker or absent mode/dissonance preferences in listeners with little Western exposure.

Context dependence: the same chord move can sound very different depending on tempo, rhythm, register, instrumentation, voicing, lyrics and what came before. Tempo and timbre often outweigh harmony for perceived emotion.

Film/genre conventions: many 'mystical', 'heroic' or 'villainous' labels (chromatic mediants, tritone progressions, Phrygian = Spanish/menace, augmented 2nd = 'exotic') are learned media conventions, some carrying orientalist baggage; the app should present them as conventions, not facts.
Consensus ratings are the compiler's judgment of how widely a description recurs across textbooks, scholarship and practitioner writing; they are not measured listener-agreement statistics.

chordMoves.name: Tonic → Subdominant (I→IV)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Opens outward from home to the subdominant. Gentle, expansive, hymn/folk/gospel feel; one of the most common moves in pop and rock.
chordMoves.consensusNote: Function (departure from tonic) is textbook; 'warm/expansive' is a widely shared but descriptive label.

chordMoves.name: Tonic → Dominant (I→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Moves to the dominant: raises energy and sets up an expectation of return. Ending a phrase here is a half cadence (open, questioning).

chordMoves.name: Tonic → Relative minor (I→vi)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Shifts to the relative minor (neo-Riemannian R): two common tones so it is smooth, but the color darkens—'the sad side of the same key'. Core of the 50s/doo-wop progression.

chordMoves.name: Tonic → Supertonic (I→ii)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Step up to the supertonic, a soft predominant that usually leads to V. Gentle and conversational; in jazz it starts the ii–V.

chordMoves.name: Tonic → Mediant (I→iii)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Shares two tones with I (neo-Riemannian L). Less common; a wistful, slightly ambiguous minor tint without leaving the key.

chordMoves.name: Subdominant → Dominant (IV→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is IV
chordMoves.description: Stepwise climb from predominant to dominant: classic build-up before a cadence; stopping here = half cadence.

chordMoves.name: Authentic cadence (V→I)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is V
chordMoves.description: The strongest resolution in tonal music: leading tone rises to tonic, root falls a fifth. Feels like arrival/closure.

chordMoves.name: Dominant seventh → Tonic (V7→I)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is V7
chordMoves.description: Adding the 7th creates a tritone (scale degrees 7 and 4) that resolves inward to 1 and 3—an even stronger pull and release than plain V→I.

chordMoves.name: Plagal 'Amen' cadence (IV→I)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is IV
chordMoves.description: Softer close than V→I with no leading tone; hymn-like ('A-men'), gospel and rock-anthem warmth.

chordMoves.name: Supertonic → Dominant (ii→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ii
chordMoves.description: Root up a fourth (down a fifth) into the dominant; the backbone of the ii–V–I and of most jazz harmony.

chordMoves.name: Relative minor → Subdominant (vi→IV)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is vi
chordMoves.description: Moves from the sad relative minor to the warm IV—the hinge of the I–V–vi–IV and vi–IV–I–V pop loops; reads as 'lifting out of sadness'.

chordMoves.name: Deceptive cadence (V→vi)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is V
chordMoves.description: The ear expects I but gets vi: the leading tone still resolves up, yet the bass steps up to 6. Classic 'twist'—prolongs the phrase with a poignant turn.

chordMoves.name: Leading-tone chord → Tonic (vii°→I)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is vii°
chordMoves.description: The diminished triad on the leading tone acts like a rootless V7; resolves smoothly by step into tonic.

chordMoves.name: Cadential 6/4 → V (I6/4→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I6/4
chordMoves.description: The tonic chord over the dominant bass delays V; the 6 and 4 above the bass fall to 5 and 3. Heightens the big moment before a final cadence (e.g., before a classical concerto cadenza).

chordMoves.name: Submediant → Supertonic (vi→ii)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is vi
chordMoves.description: Falling-fifth step in the circle progression (vi–ii–V–I); feels like a gentle, inevitable chain.

chordMoves.name: Mediant → Submediant (iii→vi)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is iii
chordMoves.description: Falling fifth between minor chords; deepens the minor shading before the chain continues to ii–V–I.

chordMoves.name: Blues/rock 'retrogression' (V→IV)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is V
chordMoves.description: Backwards from the classical point of view (dominant to predominant), but it is the standard turnaround of the 12-bar blues (V–IV–I) and countless rock songs: laid-back, rootsy.

chordMoves.name: Submediant → Dominant (vi→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is vi
chordMoves.description: Steps down from the minor vi to V; a common pop pre-chorus move that lifts toward a return to I.

chordMoves.name: Minor tonic → Minor subdominant (i→iv)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: Both chords minor: a heavy, mournful departure from home; the archetypal 'sad' predominant.

chordMoves.name: Minor tonic → Major dominant (i→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: Uses the raised 7th (harmonic minor) to make a major V with a leading tone; urgent and dramatic.

chordMoves.name: Authentic cadence in minor (V→i)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is V
chordMoves.description: Full closure, but landing on a minor tonic: final, serious, often tragic.

chordMoves.name: Minor tonic → Submediant (i→♭VI)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: A major chord that sits a semitone above the dominant: warm-but-sad, swelling; staple of cinematic and epic pop/rock minor progressions (neo-Riemannian L).

chordMoves.name: Minor tonic → Subtonic (i→♭VII)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: Natural-minor (Aeolian) whole-step down to a major chord: rock/folk modal sound, less 'classical' than i–V.

chordMoves.name: Minor tonic → Relative major (i→♭III)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: Moves to the relative major (R): a ray of light inside a minor piece.

chordMoves.name: Half-diminished supertonic → Dominant (iiø7→V7)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is iiø7
chordMoves.description: The minor-key predominant: half-diminished ii falls a fifth to V. In jazz this is the 'minor ii–V' (e.g., Bø7–E7–Am).

chordMoves.name: Minor plagal (iv→i)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is iv
chordMoves.description: Plagal close within minor: subdued, mournful, resigned.

chordMoves.name: Deceptive cadence in minor (V→♭VI)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is V
chordMoves.description: Instead of i the dominant moves up a step to the major ♭VI: a sudden warm-but-tragic swell, very effective in dramatic music.

chordMoves.name: Minor tonic → Minor dominant (i→v)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: Natural-minor v with no leading tone: modal, folk-like, less pull back home; sounds older or more pensive than i–V.

chordMoves.name: Subtonic → Minor tonic (♭VII→i)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is ♭VII
chordMoves.description: Aeolian cadence-like move: whole step up into the minor tonic without a leading tone. Rock/metal/film staple.

chordMoves.name: Submediant → Subtonic (♭VI→♭VII)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is ♭VI
chordMoves.description: Two major chords climbing by whole step: builds momentum toward the tonic (major in the 'Mario cadence', minor in Aeolian rock).

chordMoves.name: Submediant → Dominant (♭VI→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is ♭VI
chordMoves.description: Bass falls by semitone (♭6→5), the 'Phrygian' bass descent; the end of the Andalusian cadence.

chordMoves.name: Minor subdominant → Dominant (iv→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is iv
chordMoves.description: Predominant to dominant in minor. With iv in first inversion (bass ♭6→5) it is the Baroque 'Phrygian half cadence'—a sighing, unresolved pause.

chordMoves.name: Relative major → Subtonic (♭III→♭VII)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is ♭III
chordMoves.description: Falling-fifth motion between major chords inside a minor key, as in the 'epic' i–♭VI–♭III–♭VII loop.

chordMoves.name: Picardy third (i → I at the end)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: A minor-key piece ends on a MAJOR tonic: the raised third is a final ray of light. Common in Renaissance/Baroque music.

chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I

chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I

chordMoves.name: V/vi → vi (III→vi)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is III7 (V7/vi)
chordMoves.description: Resolves the applied dominant into the relative minor: a heartfelt, tearful tonicization of vi.

chordMoves.name: Tonic → V/ii (I→VI7)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Major VI7 leads to ii; the vintage sound of ragtime, barbershop and Tin Pan Alley turnarounds (I–VI7–II7–V7).

chordMoves.name: Tonic → V/IV (I→I7)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Adding a ♭7 to the tonic turns it into a dominant pointing at IV: gospel/blues warmth and forward drive.

chordMoves.name: Tonic → V/iii (I→VII)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Rarer applied dominant on the 7th degree, tonicizing iii: a striking, slightly remote color.

chordMoves.name: Applied leading-tone 7th → V (♯iv°7→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♯iv°7 (vii°7/V)
chordMoves.description: A fully diminished seventh on ♯4 resolving to V: chromatic bass rise (♯4→5) and maximum tension before a cadence.

chordMoves.name: Borrowed minor iv (I→iv)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Borrows iv from the parallel minor: the ♭6 (e.g., A♭ in C) casts a sudden wistful shadow. Neo-Riemannian 'N' (Nebenverwandt) relation.

chordMoves.name: Major IV → minor iv (IV→iv)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is IV
chordMoves.description: The 6th degree slips down a semitone (6→♭6) while the root stays: one of the most recognisable 'tear-jerker' moves in pop and film.

chordMoves.name: Minor plagal cadence (iv→I)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is iv
chordMoves.description: ♭6 falls to 5 as the borrowed iv resolves to a major tonic: a tender, 'sigh then smile' cadence.

chordMoves.name: Borrowed ♭VI (I→♭VI)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: A major chord a major third below the tonic (also a chromatic mediant, PL). Sounds grand, cinematic, sometimes dreamlike.

chordMoves.name: Borrowed ♭VII / Mixolydian (I→♭VII)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: The ♭7 (from Mixolydian/minor) gives a rock-anthem, folk, Celtic sound; removes the leading tone so it feels confident rather than pulled.

chordMoves.name: ♭VII → I (subtonic resolution)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♭VII
chordMoves.description: Whole-step rise into tonic without a leading tone: a bold, open 'rock cadence'; final chord of the Mario cadence.

chordMoves.name: ♭VI → ♭VII (in major)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♭VI
chordMoves.description: Two borrowed major chords climbing toward I: a fanfare build (video-game victory, film climaxes, power ballads).

chordMoves.name: Borrowed ♭III (I→♭III)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Major chord on ♭3: bold rock/blues color (♭3 against major tonic); also a chromatic mediant (PR).

chordMoves.name: Borrowed iiø7 (I→iiø7)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Predominant borrowed from minor: the ♭6 inside iiø7 adds a darker, more longing approach to V.

chordMoves.name: ♭VI → V (in major)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♭VI
chordMoves.description: Borrowed ♭VI slides down a semitone onto V: dramatic, operatic approach to the dominant.

chordMoves.name: ♭VI → I (in major)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♭VI
chordMoves.description: Major chord a major third below resolving directly to tonic (chromatic-mediant cadence, LP from ♭VI): radiant, cinematic arrival.

chordMoves.name: Backdoor dominant (♭VII7→I)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♭VII7
chordMoves.description: The 'backdoor' resolution (often iv7–♭VII7–I): resolves to tonic from a whole step below; mellow, sophisticated, a bit sentimental.

chordMoves.name: Mixolydian minor v (I→v)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is I
chordMoves.description: Minor v (no leading tone) borrowed from Mixolydian: relaxed, modal, 60s-rock/folk feel.

chordMoves.name: Neapolitan sixth → Dominant (♭II6→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is ♭II6 (N6)
chordMoves.description: Major chord on ♭2 (usually in first inversion) as a predominant; the ♭2 falls by diminished third toward 7. Pathos, tragedy, lament.

chordMoves.name: Minor tonic → Neapolitan (i→♭II)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is i
chordMoves.description: Root-position ♭II right after i: a semitone shift that sounds tragic in classical style and menacing/Spanish in film, flamenco and metal (Phrygian color).

chordMoves.name: Augmented sixth → Dominant (Ger+6/It+6/Fr+6→V)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a minor key, current chord is ♭VI+6 (Ger+6)
chordMoves.description: Two tendency tones (♭6 down, ♯4 up) expand outward by semitone onto the dominant octave: a powerful, wedge-like intensification typical of Romantic climaxes.

chordMoves.name: Deceptive cadence to ♭VI (V→♭VI in major)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is V
chordMoves.description: A stronger, more colorful deception than V→vi: the borrowed major ♭VI lands like a sudden scene change.

chordMoves.name: Deceptive/evaded: V → IV6
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is V
chordMoves.description: Bass steps 5→6 like a deceptive cadence but lands on IV in first inversion: a soft evasion that keeps the phrase going.

chordMoves.name: Tritone substitute → Tonic (♭II7→I)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♭II7 (subV7)
chordMoves.description: Replaces V7 with the dominant a tritone away (same tritone, enharmonically). Bass slides down a semitone into tonic: slick, chromatic, sophisticated.

chordMoves.name: ii7 → ♭II7 (approach to tritone sub)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ii7
chordMoves.description: The ii–subV–I: chromatic descending bass (2→♭2→1), smooth voice leading.

chordMoves.name: SubV/V → V (♭VI7→V7)
chordMoves.fromContext: In a major key, current chord is ♭VI7 (subV/V)
chordMoves.description: Tritone substitute for V/V; sounds like an augmented-sixth chord resolving (same notes as Ger+6).

chordMoves.fromContext: Relative to the current chord (any key); X = current root

chordMoves.name: Add the 9th (I→Iadd9)

chordMoves.name: Major seventh color (I→Imaj7)
chordMoves.fromContext: Relative to the current chord (any key); X = current root
chordMoves.description: The major 7th (a semitone below the root) softens the triad into a lush, wistful, slightly melancholic sweetness—bossa nova, soul, city-pop.

chordMoves.name: Added sixth (I→I6)
chordMoves.fromContext: Relative to the current chord (any key); X = current root
chordMoves.description: Major-sixth chord: sweet, swing-era/vintage, settled (common final chord in older jazz and pop).

chordMoves.name: Minor seventh color (i→im7)
chordMoves.fromContext: Relative to the current chord (any key); X = current root
chordMoves.description: Adding the ♭7 to a minor triad softens its sadness into something mellow, soulful and relaxed.

chordMoves.name: Minor sixth (Dorian) color (i→im6)
chordMoves.fromContext: Relative to the current chord (any key); X = current root
chordMoves.description: Minor triad with a major 6th (the Dorian note): bittersweet, noir/mysterious, gypsy-jazz flavor.

chordMoves.name: Add dominant seventh (V→V7)
chordMoves.fromContext: Relative to the current chord (any key); X = current root

chordMoves.name: Dominant 7sus4 (V7sus4→V7)

chordMoves.name: Dominant ninth (V7→V9)
chordMoves.fromContext: Relative to the current chord (any key); X = current root

chordMoves.name: Dominant 7♭9 (V7→V7♭9)

chordMoves.name: 'Hendrix chord' (V7→7♯9)

David Huron (2006), Sweet Anticipation (MIT Press), Table 9.1: scale-degree qualia

melodicMoves.name: Scale degree ♯5 (si) – Raised 5th (chromatic, augmented)
melodicMoves.description: Leans upward into 6 (augmented chords, line clichés, V/vi): aspiring, leaning, unfinished.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Major Scales, Scale Degrees, and Key Signatures
David Huron (2006), Sweet Anticipation (MIT Press), Table 9.1: scale-degree qualia

melodicMoves.name: Scale degree ♭5 (se) – Flat 5 'blue note'
melodicMoves.description: The blues scale's flat fifth, usually a passing or bent note between 4 and 5: gritty, crying, 'blue'.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Major Scales, Scale Degrees, and Key Signatures

melodicMoves.name: Repeat the note (unison)
melodicMoves.description: Repetition: emphasis, insistence, speech-like; builds anticipation when repeated rhythmically.

melodicMoves.name: Minor 2nd up
melodicMoves.description: Smallest step; creeping, menacing or straining upward (leading-tone motion).

melodicMoves.name: Minor 2nd down
melodicMoves.description: The 'sigh' (pianto) figure: a falling semitone heard as lament or gentle resolution.

melodicMoves.name: Major 2nd up
melodicMoves.description: Plain stepwise motion; the normal, conversational way melodies move.

melodicMoves.name: Major 2nd down
melodicMoves.description: Stepwise descent; relaxing, often closing (2→1).

melodicMoves.name: Minor 3rd up
melodicMoves.description: Small leap with a minor color; plaintive, folky, call-like.

sources.title: Curtis & Bharucha (2010), 'The minor third communicates sadness in speech, mirroring its use in music', Emotion 10(3)

melodicMoves.name: Minor 3rd down
melodicMoves.description: Falling minor third: the calling / playground-chant interval; Curtis & Bharucha (2010) found falling minor thirds are a key cue of sadness in speech.

sources.title: Curtis & Bharucha (2010), 'The minor third communicates sadness in speech, mirroring its use in music', Emotion 10(3)

melodicMoves.name: Major 3rd up
melodicMoves.description: Outlines a major triad: sunny, open, affirmative.

examples.title: When the Saints Go Marching In

melodicMoves.name: Major 3rd down
melodicMoves.description: Gentle, sweet descent through a major triad.

melodicMoves.name: Perfect 4th up
melodicMoves.description: Strong, purposeful upbeat leap (e.g., 5→1 pickup); fanfare-like, a 'call to attention'.

melodicMoves.name: Perfect 4th down
melodicMoves.description: Falling fourth: grounded, cadential, folk-like.

melodicMoves.name: Tritone up
melodicMoves.description: Augmented 4th: unstable, eerie, restless; nicknamed 'diabolus in musica' since at least the 18th century. Bernstein built West Side Story's 'Maria' and 'Cool' on it.

sources.title: Sharkey, Equipping the Musical Ear (LibreTexts) 6.5: Song Cues for intervals

examples.title: Maria (West Side Story)
examples.detail: Tritone featured prominently; also a standard ear-training cue

melodicMoves.name: Tritone down
melodicMoves.description: Diminished 5th: unstable, dark, unresolved.

sources.title: Sharkey, Equipping the Musical Ear (LibreTexts) 6.5: Song Cues for intervals

melodicMoves.name: Perfect 5th up
melodicMoves.description: Bold, open, heroic leap; spacious and confident.

melodicMoves.name: Perfect 5th down
melodicMoves.description: Falling fifth: grounded, conclusive (mirrors the V→I bass).

melodicMoves.name: Minor 6th up
melodicMoves.description: Wide minor leap: anguished, passionate reaching.

melodicMoves.name: Minor 6th down
melodicMoves.description: Falling minor sixth: sorrowful, heavy.

melodicMoves.name: Major 6th up
melodicMoves.description: Expansive, warm, lyrical reach; love-song leap.

examples.title: My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean

melodicMoves.name: Major 6th down
melodicMoves.description: Falling major sixth: tender, nostalgic.

examples.title: Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen

melodicMoves.name: Minor 7th up
melodicMoves.description: Very wide reach implying a dominant 7th: searching, longing; Wikipedia's Tritone article quotes a description of the 'yearning sunlight of the expansive minor seventh' in West Side Story's 'Somewhere'.

sources.title: Sharkey, Equipping the Musical Ear (LibreTexts) 6.5: Song Cues for intervals

examples.title: Somewhere (West Side Story)
examples.detail: 'There's a place for us' – rising minor 7th; described as 'yearning'

melodicMoves.name: Minor 7th down
melodicMoves.description: Falling minor seventh: dramatic plunge.

melodicMoves.name: Major 7th up
melodicMoves.description: Dissonant, straining leap that wants to continue to the octave; modern, aching.

melodicMoves.name: Major 7th down
melodicMoves.description: Jagged, dissonant drop; angular and strange.

melodicMoves.name: Octave up
melodicMoves.description: Leap to the same note higher: soaring, expansive, dreamlike opening.

melodicMoves.name: Octave down
melodicMoves.description: Drop to the same note lower: grounding, emphatic.

melodicMoves.name: Chord root
melodicMoves.description: Most stable note over any chord; landing on it confirms the harmony.

melodicMoves.name: Chord 3rd (major or minor)
melodicMoves.description: Defines the chord's quality: major 3rd sounds bright/sweet, minor 3rd sad/soft. Melodies resting on the 3rd sound expressive but settled.

melodicMoves.name: Chord 5th
melodicMoves.description: Stable and neutral/open; adds strength without color.

melodicMoves.name: ♭7 over a dominant chord
melodicMoves.description: The 7th of V7 (scale degree 4): tends to resolve down by step.

melodicMoves.name: Major 7th over a major chord
melodicMoves.description: A semitone below the root: lush, bittersweet, jazzy; as a melody note it is a hallmark of bossa nova and soul ballads.

melodicMoves.name: Added 6th (13) over a major chord
melodicMoves.description: Sweet, vintage color; very stable for a 'tension'.

melodicMoves.name: 9th (major 2nd above root)
melodicMoves.description: Soft, shimmering consonant-ish tension; resolves (9–8) or simply rings.

melodicMoves.name: ♭9 (over dominant)
melodicMoves.description: Semitone above the root: anguished, dark; wants to fall to the next chord's 5th.

melodicMoves.name: ♯9 (over dominant)
melodicMoves.description: The 'blue' minor third over a major-3rd chord: gritty, funky.

melodicMoves.name: 11th over a minor chord
melodicMoves.description: Open, modal, quartal sound (common in Dorian/funk/soul).

melodicMoves.name: Natural 11 over a major chord (avoid note)
melodicMoves.description: Clashes a minor 9th above the major 3rd; in jazz an 'avoid note' unless the chord is sus. Heard as a suspension wanting to fall to 3.

melodicMoves.name: ♯11 over a major or dominant chord
melodicMoves.description: Lydian sparkle; floating, magical, modern.

melodicMoves.name: 13th over a dominant chord
melodicMoves.description: Sweet, soulful dominant color.

melodicMoves.name: ♭13 over a dominant chord
melodicMoves.description: Pulls down toward the 5th of the next (minor) chord; dark, expressive.

melodicMoves.name: Leading tone resolves up (7→1)
melodicMoves.description: Ti→do: the archetypal resolution; satisfies the strongest tendency in the scale.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Major Scales, Scale Degrees, and Key Signatures

melodicMoves.name: Fa falls to mi (4→3)
melodicMoves.description: Resolves the 7th of V7 and the 4–3 suspension; gentle settling.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Major Scales, Scale Degrees, and Key Signatures

melodicMoves.name: La falls to sol (6→5)
melodicMoves.description: Soft resolution of the upper neighbor to 5.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Major Scales, Scale Degrees, and Key Signatures

melodicMoves.name: Le falls to sol (♭6→5)
melodicMoves.description: Semitone 'sigh' of grief/longing; core of the minor iv and minor-plagal sound.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Major Scales, Scale Degrees, and Key Signatures

melodicMoves.name: Re falls to do (2→1)
melodicMoves.description: The most common final melodic step; calm closure (Schenker's 'Urlinie' ends 2→1).

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Major Scales, Scale Degrees, and Key Signatures

melodicMoves.name: Ra falls to do (♭2→1)
melodicMoves.description: Phrygian semitone descent into tonic; heavy, fateful.

melodicMoves.name: Fi rises to sol (♯4→5)
melodicMoves.description: Applied leading tone to the dominant (V/V); a brightening push.

melodicMoves.name: Te falls to la (♭7→6)
melodicMoves.description: Relaxed modal descent (Mixolydian/Dorian flavor) instead of rising to 1.

melodicMoves.name: Blue-note bend (♭3→3)
melodicMoves.description: Minor third sliding up to major third over a major chord: blues/rock/gospel inflection.

melodicMoves.name: 4–3 suspension
melodicMoves.description: A chord tone is held over a chord change, becoming a dissonant 4th that then falls to the 3rd: tension then release.

melodicMoves.name: 9–8 suspension
melodicMoves.description: Held note becomes a 9th above the bass, then resolves down to the octave.

melodicMoves.name: 7–6 suspension
melodicMoves.description: Held 7th over a first-inversion chord resolves down to the 6th; classic in chains of sequences.

melodicMoves.name: Appoggiatura (accented leaning note)
melodicMoves.description: A dissonance on the strong beat, approached by leap and resolving by step: the 'leaning', heart-tugging gesture; studies of 'chills/tears' responses often point to appoggiaturas.

sources.title: John Sloboda (1991), 'Music Structure and Emotional Response: Some Empirical Findings', Psychology of Music 19(2)

melodicMoves.name: Passing tone
melodicMoves.description: Unaccented step connecting two chord tones; smooth, neutral motion.

melodicMoves.name: Neighbor tone (upper or lower)
melodicMoves.description: Steps away and back to the same chord tone; ornamental, decorative.

melodicMoves.name: Escape tone (échappée)
melodicMoves.description: Steps away from a chord tone then leaps in the opposite direction; a light, flicking gesture.

melodicMoves.name: Anticipation
melodicMoves.description: Arrives early on a note of the next chord; eager, forward-leaning (common at cadences and in pop syncopation).

melodicMoves.name: Chromatic passing tone
melodicMoves.description: Fills a whole step by semitones; adds slinky, sophisticated chromatic color.

melodicMoves.name: Leap then step back (gap-fill)
melodicMoves.description: After a large leap, melodies usually turn and move by step in the opposite direction; satisfying listeners' expectations (Meyer's 'gap-fill', Huron's 'post-skip reversal').

sources.title: David Huron (2006), Sweet Anticipation (MIT Press), Table 9.1: scale-degree qualia

melodicMoves.name: Step vs. leap
melodicMoves.description: Stepwise motion feels smooth and calm; leaps feel expressive, emphatic or dramatic, and larger leaps feel more effortful.

melodicMoves.name: Arpeggiate the chord
melodicMoves.description: Moving through chord tones (1–3–5) sounds stable and affirmative—fanfare/bugle-call shapes.

melodicMoves.name: Augmented 2nd (♭6→♮7 in harmonic minor)
melodicMoves.description: A 3-semitone step between ♭6 and the raised 7th; heard by Western listeners as 'exotic' (Middle-Eastern, klezmer, flamenco)—a cultural-association label, not intrinsic.

melodicMoves.name: Lydian ♯4
melodicMoves.description: Raises the 4th of major: bright, floating, magical.

melodicMoves.name: Mixolydian ♭7
melodicMoves.description: Lowers the 7th of major: rock/folk/Celtic swagger without a leading tone.

melodicMoves.name: Dorian ♮6
melodicMoves.description: Raises the 6th of natural minor: minor but brighter, cool, soulful.

melodicMoves.name: Aeolian ♭6
melodicMoves.description: The ♭6 of natural minor: sad, heavy, cinematic.

melodicMoves.name: Phrygian ♭2
melodicMoves.description: Lowers the 2nd of minor: dark, Spanish/flamenco-tinged, metal menace.

melodicMoves.name: Locrian ♭5
melodicMoves.description: Lowers the 5th: the tonic triad itself is diminished—unstable, disorienting.

melodicMoves.name: Harmonic minor ♮7
melodicMoves.description: Raised 7th in minor: leading tone + augmented 2nd; classical drama, 'exotic' flavor to Western ears.

modes.name: Lydian
modes.description: Brightest diatonic mode: major with a raised 4th. Floating, magical, 'sense of wonder'—a film-score favorite.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Introduction to Diatonic Modes

examples.title: String Quartet No. 15, Op. 132, 3rd mvt. ('Heiliger Dankgesang… in der lydischen Tonart')

modes.name: Ionian (Major)
modes.description: The major scale: bright, stable, 'happy' (for enculturated Western listeners).

modes.name: Mixolydian
modes.description: Major with a flat 7th: rock, blues, folk and Celtic; confident and relaxed rather than yearning.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Introduction to Diatonic Modes

modes.name: Dorian
modes.description: Minor with a raised 6th: melancholy but hopeful, cool, soulful; jazz, funk, folk.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Introduction to Diatonic Modes

modes.name: Aeolian (Natural minor)
modes.description: Natural minor: sad, serious, introspective; with ♭VI–♭VII it becomes epic and cinematic.

modes.name: Phrygian
modes.description: Minor with a flat 2nd: dark, tense, Spanish/flamenco and metal associations.

sources.title: Open Music Theory (v2): Introduction to Diatonic Modes

modes.name: Locrian
modes.description: Darkest diatonic mode: diminished tonic, no stable perfect fifth. Unsettled, rarely a true 'home'.

modes.name: Harmonic minor
modes.description: Minor with a raised 7th: classical drama, leading tone, and an augmented 2nd heard as 'exotic' in Western contexts.

modes.name: Melodic minor (jazz minor)
modes.description: Minor with raised 6 and 7: smooth, sophisticated; source of the minor-major 7th and altered/Lydian-dominant sounds.

modes.name: Phrygian dominant
modes.description: 5th mode of harmonic minor: flamenco, klezmer, Middle-Eastern-associated; intense and dramatic.

modes.name: Lydian dominant (acoustic scale)
modes.description: Lydian with a ♭7: bright yet bluesy, whimsical; heard in jazz and some TV/film themes.

modes.name: Major pentatonic
modes.description: No semitones: open, innocent, folk-like; found in many musical cultures worldwide.

modes.name: Minor pentatonic
modes.description: Basis of blues and rock soloing: soulful, gritty, easy to improvise with.

modes.name: Blues scale
modes.description: Minor pentatonic plus ♭5: gritty, crying blue-note color.

modes.name: Whole-tone
modes.description: Symmetrical, no leading tone or perfect fifth: hazy, dream-sequence, impressionist (Debussy) sound.

examples.title: Voiles (Préludes, Book 1)
examples.detail: Almost entirely within one whole-tone scale

modes.name: Octatonic (diminished)
modes.description: Symmetrical half-whole scale: tense, magical, dangerous (Rimsky-Korsakov, Stravinsky, jazz over 7♭9 chords, film suspense).
